questions.question: What is the primary difference between single-subject research and group research?

answers.text: Single-subject research studies a small number of participants intensively, while group research studies large numbers and focuses on group statistics
Single-subject research is qualitative, while group research is quantitative
Single-subject research uses surveys, while group research uses experiments
Single-subject research has lower internal validity than group research

questions.question: In the study by Hall and colleagues, what was the treatment used to increase students' studying behavior?

answers.text: Giving students extra homework assignments
Positive attention from the teacher, such as comments like 'good work' or a pat on the shoulder
Removing disruptive students from the classroom
Providing monetary rewards for completing schoolwork

questions.question: What does the term 'social validity' refer to in single-subject research?

answers.text: The ability to generalize results to different social groups
Strong and consistent effects that can be implemented reliably in real-world contexts
The extent to which participants accept the researcher socially
Statistical validity when analyzing social behavior

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an assumption underlying single-subject research?

answers.text: It is important to focus intensively on individual participants
Large sample sizes are necessary to detect treatment effects
Causal relationships should be discovered through experimental manipulation
It is important to study strong and consistent effects with biological or social importance

questions.question: What is the 'steady state strategy' in single-subject research?

answers.text: Keeping all conditions constant throughout the study
Waiting until the participant's behavior becomes fairly consistent before changing conditions
Maintaining a fixed schedule for introducing treatments
Ensuring participants remain in the same emotional state

questions.question: In an ABA reversal design, what does the first 'A' phase represent?

answers.text: The treatment phase
A baseline condition before treatment is introduced
An alternating treatment condition
The final assessment phase

questions.question: Why is the reversal (removal of treatment) considered necessary in reversal designs?

answers.text: To save time and resources during the study
To increase the internal validity by showing that changes are due to the treatment, not extraneous variables
To ensure participants do not become dependent on the treatment
To meet ethical requirements for research

questions.question: In a multiple-baseline design across participants, when is the treatment introduced?

answers.text: At the same time for all participants
At different times for each participant
Only after all baselines are completely stable
Randomly throughout the study period

questions.question: What was the key finding in Ross and Horner's study on bullying prevention?

answers.text: Aggressive behaviors increased after the program was implemented
Aggressive behaviors dropped shortly after the program was implemented at each school
The program had no effect on bullying behavior
Only one school showed improvement in student behavior

questions.question: In a multiple-baseline design across behaviors, what is varied?

answers.text: The participants receiving treatment
The dependent variables for the same participant, with treatment introduced at different times
The type of treatment used
The duration of each baseline phase

questions.question: What is 'visual inspection' in single-subject research?

answers.text: Using video recordings to analyze participant behavior
Plotting individual data graphically and making judgments about treatment effects
Observing participants through one-way mirrors
Conducting statistical analyses using visualization software

questions.question: Which factor is NOT typically considered when visually inspecting single-subject data?

answers.text: Changes in level from condition to condition
Trend (gradual increases or decreases)
Sample size requirements
Latency (time for change to occur after condition change)

questions.question: What does PND (percentage of non-overlapping data) measure?

answers.text: The percentage of participants who showed improvement
The percentage of responses in treatment that are more extreme than the most extreme response in control
The percentage of time the dependent variable was measured
The statistical significance level of the treatment effect

questions.question: Who is considered a founder of single-subject research methodology in the mid-20th century?

answers.text: Sigmund Freud
B. F. Skinner
Carl Rogers
Jean Piaget

questions.question: What is 'applied behavior analysis'?

answers.text: A subfield using single-subject research primarily with humans in applied settings
A statistical method for analyzing group data
A qualitative approach to studying behavior
A theoretical perspective focused on unconscious processes

questions.question: In an alternating treatments design, how are treatments presented?

answers.text: One treatment is used for the entire study
Two or more treatments are alternated relatively quickly on a regular schedule
Treatments are introduced in random order over months
Multiple treatments are given simultaneously

questions.question: What is one potential problem with reversal designs mentioned in the chapter?

answers.text: They require too many participants
It may be unethical to remove a working treatment, or the dependent variable may not return to baseline
They cannot establish causal relationships
They are too expensive to conduct

questions.question: According to the chapter, what concern do single-subject researchers have about group research data analysis?

answers.text: Group means can be misleading when treatment effects differ across individuals
Group research never uses statistical analysis
Group research cannot measure dependent variables reliably
Group research always lacks internal validity

questions.question: What is the 'principle of converging evidence'?

answers.text: Conducting the same study multiple times with identical methods
Examining patterns across multiple studies with different strengths and weaknesses to increase confidence in conclusions
Using only experimental designs to establish causation
Focusing exclusively on statistically significant findings

questions.question: How did single-subject research contribute to understanding the 'number sense'?

answers.text: By showing that only humans possess mathematical abilities
By demonstrating similar abilities in animals and human infants to discriminate small numbers
By proving that number sense must be taught through education
By establishing that number sense develops only in adulthood
